The prize scores proposals on a published state vector of 25+ variables (cost-effectiveness, welfare impact, political feasibility, capture resistance, and completeness) and awards not cash but adoption capital, political support, distribution, and operating rights. ## Introduction

If this manual is the least bad idea on Earth, implement it. If it is not, replace it immediately with something better. The point is not to marry a blueprint. The point is to stop subsidizing death, disease, waste, and suffering.

The cost of the current approach is not abstract. {{< var existing_drugs_efficacy_lag_deaths_total_nounit >}} people have already died waiting for drugs that were proven to work but stuck in regulatory queues. The annual economic burden of treatable disease runs {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}}. The total opportunity cost of political dysfunction (the gap between what governance delivers and what it could deliver) is {{< var political_dysfunction_global_opportunity_cost_total >}} per year. Those are not projections. They are the running tab for not having a mechanism that selects and implements better ideas.

That suggests a simple rule: stop treating policy design like a philosophy seminar and start treating it like an engineering competition.

Create a **standing prize** for the first person, team, or institution that can **cause the implementation** of every required function in the Earth Optimization Plan from the companion papers [@value-captured-by-1pct-treaty; @iab-paper-2025; @wishocracy-paper-2025; @optimocracy-paper-2025; @opg-paper-2025; @obg-paper-2025; @dfda-impact-paper-2025; @invisible-graveyard-paper-2025; @political-dysfunction-tax-paper-2025; @cost-of-change-paper-2025; @us-efficiency-audit-paper-2025; @dfda-spec-paper-2025; @drug-development-cost], or a strict module-by-module improvement on it, while delivering a **lower verified cost per DALY**, lower suffering per dollar, and better net outcomes for living beings.

Not a trophy. Not a TED Talk. Not "best essay wins." A market for verified implementation.

Here is the inevitability theorem in one sentence: a machine that selects the best available mechanism and replaces itself when beaten is, by construction, at least as good as any mechanism it could select. The only way to beat the prize is to produce something better, and producing something better is the entire point. This paper describes that machine.

::: {.callout-important}
## Disqualification Rule

If your proposal requires politicians, bureaucrats, investors, regulators, voters, or interest groups to become less selfish than they are now, you have not designed a mechanism. You have written fan fiction.
:::

**How to read this paper.** It does three things: defines what "better" means with a published scorecard, describes the current best candidate and how it achieves its numbers, and explains why a prize is the right selection mechanism. If you want the mechanism before the formalism, skip to [How the Earth Optimization Plan Achieves Its Numbers](#how-the-plan-achieves-its-numbers).

## Why Current Systems Fail

The political economy of public goods provision is governed by what Olson [-@olson1965] called the logic of collective action. Concentrated interests (defense contractors, entrenched pharmaceutical monopolies, legacy energy conglomerates) face high per-capita stakes in policy outcomes, so they easily overcome coordination costs to fund sustained lobbying. Diffuse beneficiaries (the general public dying of untreated diseases, bearing the cost of regulatory delay, or subsidizing low-return military spending) have tiny individual stakes in any single policy fight and cannot coordinate a proportional response.

This persists despite a massive underlying capital asymmetry. Global household wealth totals {{< var global_household_wealth_usd >}}, compared to {{< var concentrated_interest_sector_market_cap_usd >}} held by concentrated opposition sectors. The public has the money. It does not have the coordination mechanism. Politicians know which programs have high benefit-cost ratios and which do not. They fund the low-return programs anyway, because in the current equilibrium the concentrated cost of opposing a lobby exceeds the diffuse benefit of pleasing an uncoordinated public [@iab-paper-2025].

The prize exists because no existing meta-mechanism solves this at the right level. Prediction markets tell you what will win; they do not cause implementation. DAOs suffer the same Olsonian capture: whoever buys the most tokens sets the agenda. Expert committees are capturable by definition. A prize with published scoring, adversarial challenges, and automatic replacement is the one structure where capturing it requires beating every challenger on 28 verified metrics simultaneously. That is not capture-proof. But it is capture-expensive, which is probably the best available.

## The Rule

To win the prize, a proposal must clear six tests:

1. **Implementation, not commentary.** It must produce actual budget reallocations, legal adoption, institutional deployment, or binding coordination, not just a white paper and a podcast circuit.
2. **Complete Earth Optimization Plan or strict dominance.** It must implement every required function in this project, or replace each omitted function with a strictly dominating substitute on outcome, feasibility, and durability.
3. **Lower verified cost per DALY.** If it saves fewer lives per dollar than the Earth Optimization Plan, it loses. If it reduces DALYs cheaply by dumping suffering onto voiceless creatures, it also loses.
4. **Net welfare improvement across affected beings.** A qualifying plan must not merely move pain from one ledger to another. Offloading harm onto foreigners, future people, patients without bargaining power, or nonhuman animals is disqualification, not cleverness.
5. **Reallocation from low NSV to high NSV.** The mechanism must redirect resources from uses with low or negative net societal value into uses with higher verified returns.
6. **Greed-monotone public-choice compatibility.** Every critical actor must have a selfish reason to cooperate, and stronger self-interest should make the mechanism stronger rather than weaker: investors, politicians, bureaucrats, validators, operators, and ordinary citizens.

The "least bad" language matters. You are not waiting for perfection. You are asking a more adult question: *which implementable mechanism beats the alternatives once actual humans touch it?*

## Better Needs Units

Right now "better" is too vague. A real prize needs a published state vector.

These are the minimum variables the prize should score:

| Symbol | What it measures | Why it belongs in the prize | Current anchor from the papers |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `C_total` | Total all-in adoption cost | Political feasibility is a cost question, not a vibes question | Treaty path: {{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}}; global upper-bound framing from *Price of Political Change* [@cost-of-change-paper-2025]: ~$200B |
| `P_success` | Probability of binding adoption and sustained implementation | Expected value matters more than conditional fantasy | Conservative central estimate in the Earth Optimization Plan: {{< var political_success_probability >}} |
| `T_first` | Time to first binding implementation | Delay kills; speed is part of the prize | Right-to-Trial act implies concrete clocks: 180 days, 1 year, 18 months |
| `R_shift` | Annual dollars redirected from lower NSV uses to higher NSV uses | The point is resource reallocation, not rhetorical victory | First legible benchmark: {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year |
| `NSV_gain` | Annual net societal value recovered | Prize should measure recovered value, not just gross spending | Global ceiling: {{< var political_dysfunction_global_opportunity_cost_total >}}/year; U.S. waste map: {{< var us_gov_waste_total >}}/year |
| `CE_conditional` | Cost per DALY if adopted | Measures the physics/economics of the policy itself | Treaty path benchmark: {{< var treaty_cost_per_daly_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}}/DALY |
| `CE_expected` | Risk-adjusted cost per DALY = `C_total / (P_success * DALY_net)` | Measures the politics plus the policy | Earth Optimization Plan benchmark: {{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY |
| `DALY_net` | Net DALYs averted | Core welfare output from the health papers | Earth Optimization Plan medical benchmark: {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_dalys_nounit >}} DALYs |
| `H_suffering` | Suffering hours averted | DALYs hide suffering intensity; the prize should not | Earth Optimization Plan medical benchmark: {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_suffering_hours_nounit >}} hours |
| `D_avoided` | Deaths averted | Humans understand body counts faster than DALYs | Timeline-shift benchmark: {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved_nounit >}} deaths; historical lag burden: {{< var existing_drugs_efficacy_lag_deaths_total_nounit >}} deaths |
| `gIncome_med` | Change in real after-tax median income growth | Optimocracy [@optimocracy-paper-2025], OPG [@opg-paper-2025], and OBG [@obg-paper-2025] treat this as the core income-side welfare metric | Must be reported directly from causal evidence; GDP per capita is not a substitute |
| `Y_avg_20` | Average income (GDP per capita) at year 20 | The current macro path model expresses ceiling context in per-capita output levels, so keep that separate from the median-income metric | Year-20 calibration anchors: Earth {{< var current_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}}, Treaty {{< var treaty_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}}, Wishonia {{< var wishonia_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}} |
| `dHealthy_med` | Change in median healthy life years | The second terminal welfare metric in the governance papers | Must be reported explicitly even when evidence comes through surrogate outcomes |
| `Q_budget` | Budget evidence quality | Major spending shifts need a confidence score, not a slogan | OBG's Budget Impact Score (BIS) [@obg-paper-2025] |
| `Q_policy` | Policy evidence quality | Law/regulation changes need a causal score | OPG's Policy Impact Score (PIS) [@opg-paper-2025] |
| `Q_signal` | Medical signal quality | Medical claims need causal triage before trial escalation | dFDA Predictor Impact Score (PIS) [@dfda-spec-paper-2025] |
| `Q_trial` | Trial-priority quality | The prize should know which validated signals deserve scarce experimental slots | Trial Priority Score = PIS x DALYs x Novelty x Feasibility |
| `A_pref` | Preference-alignment score | If the mechanism claims democratic legitimacy, measure it | Wishocracy Citizen Alignment Score [@wishocracy-paper-2025] |
| `I_actor_min` | Minimum utility delta across key actors | If any required actor is net worse off, the mechanism is probably fiction | Earth Optimization Plan anchors: {{< var victory_bond_annual_return_pct >}} investor upside, {{< var iab_mechanism_benefit_cost_ratio >}} mechanism BCR, {{< var global_household_wealth_usd >}} vs {{< var concentrated_interest_sector_market_cap_usd >}} coordination asymmetry |
| `R_capture` | Capture/manipulation risk | Every serious governance mechanism gets attacked | Optimocracy's whole point is to collapse many attack surfaces into a few expensive ones [@optimocracy-paper-2025] |
| `B_rights` | Hard blocking-factor count | A plan that improves averages by violating rights is not a win | OPG explicitly treats freedom/autonomy constraints as blockers [@opg-paper-2025] |
| `W_sentient_net` | Net welfare across all affected sentient beings | Prevents fake wins that export suffering to weaker populations or animals | Must stay positive for humans, future people, and nonhuman animals on net |
| `W_class_min` | Welfare change for the worst-off affected class of living or sentient beings | Aggregate gains are not enough if any major class is sacrificed | Operational rule: humans, future humans, nonhuman animals, and affected living systems must each be non-negative on the best available model |
| `M_complete` | Baseline-bundle completion score | Prevents narrow proposals from winning by solving only one bottleneck | Grand prize requires 100% coverage of the required-function bundle below |
| `L_bind` | Binding-force score | A plan is not implemented until it controls law, budgets, institutions, or enforceable contracts | Binding examples in the Earth Optimization Plan: treaty, statute, agency rule, PAC-financed scorecards, auditable contracts |
| `J_cov` | Jurisdictional and population coverage | Pilot success is not system implementation | Must scale to enough authority, budget, and population to match or beat baseline `R_shift` |
| `T_full` | Time to full-bundle deployment | Time to first win is not time to complete Earth Optimization Plan implementation | Measured from launch until every required function is live or dominated |
| `D_durable` | Durability under hostile turnover | A plan that dies after one election is not implemented | Must survive leadership change, budget challenge, and organized opposition |
| `G_monotone` | Minimum marginal effect of actor self-interest on success | The greedier humans are, the better this should work | Must stay positive for investors, politicians, operators, validators, and citizens |
| `F_reinvest` | Fraction of recovered value automatically recycled into remaining missing modules | Early wins must finance completion of the Earth Optimization Plan rather than stopping at a local maximum | IAB/prize-treasury logic implies positive contractual recycling [@iab-paper-2025] |

That is the minimum scoreboard. Anything less is still just literary criticism with a grant budget.

## The Baseline Bundle

This prize is not comparing proposals to isolated papers one at a time. The canonical object to beat is the **integrated bundle of required functions** implied by the companion papers.

| Required function | Default implementation in the Earth Optimization Plan | What a strict improvement must beat |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Large initial reallocation wedge | **The 1% Treaty** [@value-captured-by-1pct-treaty] | Must redirect at least as much low-NSV spending to higher-NSV use, or achieve better welfare with less |
| Medical throughput and evidence generation | **Ubiquitous Pragmatic Trial Impact Analysis** [@dfda-impact-paper-2025] + **The Continuous Evidence Generation Protocol** [@dfda-spec-paper-2025] | Must produce faster, cheaper, more reliable treatment discovery and validation |
| Regulatory-delay removal | **The Invisible Graveyard** [@invisible-graveyard-paper-2025] + **Right to Trial & FDA Upgrade Act** + **Drug Development Cost Increase Analysis** [@drug-development-cost] | Must reduce efficacy lag and development cost at least as well without increasing net harm |
| Political financing and adoption engine | **Incentive Alignment Bonds** [@iab-paper-2025] | Must make passage and enforcement at least as incentive-compatible for selfish actors |
| Citizen preference aggregation | **Wishocracy** [@wishocracy-paper-2025] | Must recover public preference intensity at equal or lower cognitive and organizational cost |
| Waste and opportunity accounting | **The Political Dysfunction Tax** [@political-dysfunction-tax-paper-2025] + **United States Efficiency Audit** [@us-efficiency-audit-paper-2025] | Must identify low-NSV pools and recoverable value at least as well |
| Policy recommendation engine | **Optimocracy** [@optimocracy-paper-2025] + **The Optimal Policy Generator** [@opg-paper-2025] | Must generate better enact/replace/repeal/maintain recommendations under real-world constraints |
| Budget recommendation engine | **The Optimal Budget Generator** [@obg-paper-2025] | Must allocate public-goods spending better on the terminal welfare metrics |
| Legal and institutional implementation path | **Right to Trial & FDA Upgrade Act** + treaty/statutory machinery | Must create equal or stronger binding force in law, budget control, or institutional design |
| Narrative, coalition, and sequencing wrapper | **How to End War and Disease** | Must coordinate adoption at equal or lower cost and failure risk |

That is the baseline bundle. The grand prize is for the first mechanism that covers **every row** in that table or replaces any row with a strictly better module.

## How the Earth Optimization Plan Achieves Its Numbers {#how-the-plan-achieves-its-numbers}

The numbers in the thresholds below sound implausible until you see the mechanisms. Here is enough to evaluate whether each benchmark is credible, in pipeline order.

The full loop: military budgets shrink by 1%, the freed {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year funds pragmatic trials at {{< var recovery_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} lower cost per patient, those trials discover treatments years faster, the treatments save lives and generate economic returns, those returns pay investors who funded the political campaign to pass the treaty, and media coverage of cures creates voter demand that makes expansion easier than repeal. Each stage feeds the next. That feedback loop is why the numbers compound rather than stall.

**The reallocation source.** The 1% Treaty redirects {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year by coordinating every signatory to cut the same 1% of military spending simultaneously ({{< var global_military_spending_annual_2024 >}} globally). No new taxes. The game theory is stable because proportional reduction preserves relative deterrence. The economic logic is straightforward: military spending beyond deterrence returns roughly 0.7:1 on welfare; medical research returns 100:1+. The treaty moves money from the worst line item to the best one.

**The medical bottleneck.** Current clinical trials cost {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}/patient and exclude 86% of the population, producing a {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}} backlog to clear 6,650 untreated diseases. Pragmatic trials embedded in routine care cost {{< var dfda_pragmatic_trial_cost_per_patient >}}/patient (the RECOVERY trial found dexamethasone in {{< var oxford_recovery_trial_duration_months >}} for {{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}}/patient and saved {{< var recovery_trial_global_lives_saved >}} [@recovery-cost-500; @recovery-trial-1m-lives-saved]). At treaty funding through that cheaper infrastructure, the queue drops to {{< var dfda_queue_clearance_years >}}. Meanwhile, {{< var existing_drugs_efficacy_lag_deaths_total_nounit >}} people died waiting an average of {{< var efficacy_lag_years >}} for drugs that were already proven to work but stuck in regulatory queues [@bio-clinical-development-2021]. Right to Trial eliminates that lag by allowing conditional access after Phase I safety data.

**The political adoption engine.** Incentive Alignment Bonds flip the Olsonian equilibrium through three layers: an independent organization scores politicians on net-social-value voting records, PACs support high-scorers and oppose low-scorers, and foundations guarantee post-office careers for champions. Voting for high-NSV programs becomes the career-maximizing choice. Investor returns ({{< var victory_bond_annual_return_pct >}} annually) come from revenue share of treaty-generated funding flows, not from magic; the benefit-cost ratio of the mechanism itself is {{< var iab_mechanism_benefit_cost_ratio >}} [@iab-paper-2025].

**The waste map.** The Political Dysfunction Tax ({{< var political_dysfunction_global_opportunity_cost_total >}}/year) is not a spending figure. It is the gap between actual output and optimal-governance output, aggregating a waste ledger (military overspend, healthcare administration, regulatory burden) and an opportunity ledger (delayed cures, migration barriers, lead poisoning). The US Efficiency Audit itemizes {{< var us_gov_waste_total >}}/year across ten categories; the three largest are healthcare administration, housing policy failure, and excess military spending [@us-efficiency-audit-paper-2025; @political-dysfunction-tax-paper-2025].

**Preference aggregation.** Wishocracy asks citizens to drag a slider between two random budget priorities ("Nuclear modernization vs. clinical trials?"). About 20 comparisons, 5 minutes. Random pairs prevent gaming. Statistical models (Bradley-Terry, PageRank) aggregate millions of pairwise judgments into budget-preference weights without speeches, lobbying, or horse-trading. Crowds consistently outperform expert panels on preference recovery [@wishocracy-paper-2025].

None of these mechanisms require inventing new physics. The Montreal Protocol coordinated proportional reduction across nations and worked. PEPFAR redirected tens of billions of dollars into health and saved millions of lives. The RECOVERY trial proved pragmatic trials deliver at {{< var recovery_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} lower cost per patient. The open question is not whether coordinated reallocation, pragmatic trials, or incentive-aligned political financing work individually. It is whether combining them into a single plan, selected and funded via prize, produces better results than deploying them separately or not at all.

## The Completeness Rule

The grand prize is not for the cheapest local patch. It is for the first mechanism that closes the whole loop from diagnosis to reallocation to durable implementation.

1. Every required function in the baseline bundle must be implemented directly or replaced by a dominating substitute.
2. A substitute counts as dominating only if it weakly improves cost per DALY, suffering reduction, coverage, durability, and greed-compatibility relative to the module it replaces, and strictly improves at least one of those dimensions.
3. Partial packages may win milestone bounties, but they do not win the grand prize.
4. If a proposal begins with only part of the bundle live, a fixed share of verified recovered value must be contractually routed into the remaining missing functions until `M_complete = 1` or every missing function has a certified dominating substitute.

The papers already imply concrete floors, ceilings, and sanity checks:

To put the cost-effectiveness threshold in context:

| Intervention | Cost per DALY averted |
|:---|:---|
| Malaria bed nets (current gold standard) | {{< var bed_nets_cost_per_daly >}} |
| 1% Treaty (conditional, if adopted) | {{< var treaty_cost_per_daly_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}} |
| 1% Treaty (risk-adjusted, {{< var political_success_probability >}} success) | {{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}} |

Any proposal that cannot beat the risk-adjusted treaty benchmark on cost per DALY, or clearly dominate it on other welfare dimensions, does not get scored.

## The Admissibility Rule

A proposal should not even enter the final ranking unless all of these are true:

$$
W_{sentient,net} > 0
$$

$$
B_{rights} = 0
$$

$$
W_{class,min} \ge 0
$$

$$
M_{complete} = 1
$$

$$
L_{bind} > 0
$$

$$
G_{monotone} > 0
$$

$$
F_{reinvest} > 0
$$

$$
J_{cov} \ge J_{baseline}
$$

$$
D_{durable} \ge D_{min}
$$

$$
I_{actor,min} > 0
$$

$$
R_{shift} > 0
$$

$$
CE_{expected} \le CE_{baseline,best}
$$

Here $J_{baseline}$ means enough authority, budget, and population coverage to match or beat the baseline bundle's implementation footprint, and $D_{min}$ means at least two election cycles or equivalent treaty/contractual lock-in. Those are the no-loophole clauses: no sacrificed class, no missing module, no non-binding pilot, and no mechanism that gets worse when humans act selfishly.

## Welfare Accounting Protocol

The welfare guardrails above should not be interpreted as poetic aspirations. They need an explicit accounting rule.

Every serious proposal should publish a **class-by-class impact table** with at least these rows:

- present humans
- future humans
- nonhuman animals directly affected
- nonhuman animals indirectly affected through land use, food systems, or ecological spillovers
- affected living systems whose degradation plausibly creates durable downstream suffering

For each class, the submission should report:

- direct expected welfare change
- lower-bound welfare change under conservative assumptions
- main uncertainty sources
- irreversibility risk
- rights/blocking-factor flags
- proposed mitigation or compensation path if the lower bound is near zero

The operational rule is simple:

1. **Use lower bounds, not central estimates, for admissibility.** If a class looks positive only on optimistic assumptions, the proposal is not yet admissible.
2. **Price uncertainty against the proposal.** Unknown but plausible severe harms count as negative until measurement improves.
3. **Keep rights as hard constraints.** A proposal does not buy its way out of coercion, fraud, or autonomy violations by producing a large aggregate gain elsewhere.
4. **Separate welfare from money.** Economic equivalents are useful for scale intuition, but they do not substitute for DALYs, suffering, mortality, or class-specific welfare accounting.

That is how `W_sentient_net`, `W_class_min`, and `B_rights` stop being slogans and become auditable gates.

## The Ranking Rule

Among admissible proposals, rank them by something like:

$$
PrizeScore = \frac{P_{success} \times NSV_{gain} \times Q_{evidence}}{C_{total}}
$$

Where $Q_{evidence}$ is a normalized confidence-and-implementability term built from the project's own scoring machinery:

$$
Q_{evidence} = \text{geometric mean}(Q_{budget}, Q_{policy}, Q_{signal}, Q_{trial}, A_{pref}, L_{bind})
$$

Operationally, the ranking should be read **lexicographically**, not as one sloppy scalar:

1. Clear admissibility.
2. Maximize expected suffering reduction and DALYs averted per dollar.
3. Then maximize risk-adjusted `NSV_gain / C_total` among proposals that are already near-indistinguishable on the terminal welfare metrics.

That ordering matters. It prevents a growth-heavy or fiscally impressive proposal from outranking a clearly better suffering-reduction package merely because it produces larger dollar denominators.

Then use tie-breakers in this order:

1. Lower `CE_expected`
2. Higher `W_class_min` and `W_sentient_net`
3. Shorter `T_full` and `T_first`
4. Lower `R_capture`
5. Higher `dHealthy_med` and `gIncome_med`
6. Higher `G_monotone` and `F_reinvest`

That gives you a prize that can actually pick a winner instead of just admiring prose.

## The Prize Is a Machine, Not a Check

A normal prize gives someone cash after they do something impressive. That is fine for building a better battery. It is useless for governance reform, because the hard part is not inventing the idea. The hard part is forcing implementation through institutions designed to resist it.

So the prize has to award the thing that matters:

- **Adoption capital.** The leading proposal gets access to the financing infrastructure needed to pass it.
- **Distribution.** The leading proposal becomes the default object of campaign messaging, coalition outreach, and referendum traffic.
- **Political support.** Politicians who adopt the leading proposal get scored, promoted, and financed through the same incentive machinery described in the companion papers.
- **Operating rights.** The winning implementation team gets the prestige, contracts, revenue share, or administrative role attached to actually making the system work.
- **Completion covenant.** A fixed share of verified recovered value is automatically routed into any still-missing baseline functions until the whole bundle is live or every missing function is replaced by a dominating substitute.
- **Independent escrow and recertification.** Prize capital sits in an auditable treasury with published scoring, challenge windows, and periodic re-ranking so capture cannot freeze a bad winner in place.
- **Automatic replacement.** If a superior proposal appears later, the prize funding and political support migrate to that one instead.

That last point is the whole trick. The prize does not defend any particular proposal against better ideas. It weaponizes better ideas against inertia.

The treasury should normally bootstrap via **assurance contracts**, not discretionary fundraising. Pledges are committed only if the funding threshold is reached; otherwise they are not called or are returned. That is enough to let donors and organizations support the prize conditionally without taking open-ended balance-sheet risk. If a seed sponsor wants even stronger early-coordination pressure, it can add a **dominant-assurance tranche** [@tabarrok1998]. In that case the failure bonus must come from a separately pre-funded underwriting reserve. It is not magic, and it is not charged to later pledgers by default.

## Prize Constitution

To make the phrase "causes implementation" mean something, the prize needs a constitution, not just a mission statement.

At minimum, that constitution should define five roles:

1. **Treasury trustee.** Holds capital in escrow and may release it only by the published deployment rule.
2. **Measurement layer.** Independent auditors score admissibility and rank proposals against the published state vector.
3. **Challenge layer.** Adversaries can dispute any score by posting a challenge bond and submitting contrary evidence.
4. **Deployment layer.** The operational arm that routes campaign capital, media support, contracting authority, and coalition traffic to the top-ranked admissible package.
5. **Recertification layer.** Periodically re-scores the winner so the machine can replace it when something better appears.

The constitutional rules should be equally blunt:

- **No ordinary override.** No board, founder, donor, or politician may keep capital on a lower-ranked package just because they prefer it.
- **Automatic migration trigger.** If the current winner loses admissibility or is strictly beaten on the published rule for a full review cycle, funding and support move automatically.
- **Emergency pause is narrow.** The only valid pause grounds are fraud, rights violations, or newly discovered severe downside risk, and a pause must trigger immediate public re-review rather than quiet discretion.
- **Deployment waterfall is mandatory.** Idle capital is a design failure. Treasury funds must continuously route to the highest-ranked admissible implementation opportunity.

That is the missing bridge between "great selection rule" and "actual institutional ratchet."

## Protocol Adoption by Existing Organizations

The best dissemination model is not "every organization invents its own prize from scratch." That creates fragmentation, incompatible scoring, and easy capture. The best model is **many instances, one protocol**.

The protocol is the non-negotiable part:

- the constitution
- the admissibility rule
- the ranking rule
- the audit standard
- the automatic-replacement rule

An instance is the local wrapper around that protocol:

- a branded fundraising campaign
- a jurisdiction-specific treasury
- a domain-specific tranche
- an implementation partnership in one country, state, or sector

That distinction matters because it lets many organizations participate without making the mechanism incoherent.

Organizations should be able to adopt the prize in at least three modes:

1. **Endorser.** Publishes, promotes, and recruits for the prize protocol but does not hold treasury funds or underwrite failure payments.
2. **Sponsor.** Raises money into independent escrow under the shared rules, but does not control scoring or payout migration.
3. **Deployment partner.** Helps execute the winning package and can earn contracts, fees, or outcome-side compensation only if real implementation happens.

This is also where the `$0 or negative cost` question becomes operational. A host organization can participate at roughly zero or negative net cost if all of the following are true:

1. **Treasury funds stay off the host balance sheet.** Pledges go to independent escrow rather than the organization's operating account.
2. **Ops funding is explicit and capped.** A small admin, audit, and marketing reserve is funded first out of pledged capital under published limits.
3. **Failure underwriting is external.** If a dominant-assurance seed tranche is used, a separate sponsor funds the failure reserve; the host organization does not absorb it by default.
4. **No threshold, no treasury call.** If the funding threshold is not met, pledged funds are not called or are returned.
5. **Host upside is rule-bound.** The host may receive a fixed admin fee, donor-acquisition upside, or capped deployment compensation, but not discretionary control over ranking or payout.

Under that structure, an endorser can participate at near-zero cost, a sponsor can avoid fronting treasury risk, and a deployment partner can have negative net cost if reimbursements, donor growth, or implementation fees exceed marginal staff time.

The anti-fragmentation rule should therefore be blunt: an organization may brand and market its own instance, but it should not call it part of this prize family unless it accepts the same core protocol and the same automatic migration to better admissible proposals. Many storefronts are good. Many constitutions are not.

### Why Hosting Is Rational

Organizations do not make decisions. Humans inside organizations do. So the relevant question is not "does the abstract institution benefit?" but "what is the expected net benefit to the humans deciding whether to host an instance?"

The project's own model gives a lower-bound answer. If the full Earth Optimization Plan or something better is implemented, the modeled lifetime per-capita income gain is {{< var wishonia_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}}. A more conservative floor using only the treaty path is still {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}}. Those are not organizational accounting gains; they are modeled gains to the humans making the decision.

The simplest host-side matrix is therefore:

| Human choice inside the host organization | If implementation happens somewhere | If implementation does not happen |
|---|---|---|
| Create a compatible prize instance | Gain the same human-level implementation benefit as everyone else, roughly {{< var wishonia_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} on the full path or {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} on the conservative floor, plus any host-side donor, fee, or relevance upside | Roughly zero or slightly positive if host costs are reimbursed and the instance still generates learning, donor growth, or coalition-building |
| Do not create a prize instance | Gain the implementation benefit only if other people do the work first | Zero, while the probability of implementation remains lower and delay continues to destroy value |

That table is intentionally simple, but it still hides the main causal point: creating an instance is valuable because it can increase the probability of implementation and speed the date at which implementation happens. For a human decision-maker, the expected incremental value of creating a compatible instance rather than abstaining is approximately:

$$
\Delta EV_{host} \approx \Delta p \cdot B_{person} + p_{create} \cdot H_{host} + (1-p_{create}) \cdot L_{host} - C_{host}
$$

where $\Delta p$ is the increase in implementation probability caused by hosting an instance, $B_{person}$ is the human-level benefit if the plan is implemented, $H_{host}$ is any additional host-side upside if implementation happens, $L_{host}$ is any residual learning or donor value if it does not, and $C_{host}$ is the host's true unreimbursed cost.

In direct personal-value terms, even tiny probability changes are worth real money:

| Increase in implementation probability caused by the instance | Personal expected value using the treaty-only floor ({{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}}) | Personal expected value using the full path ({{< var wishonia_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}}) |
|---|---|---|
| `0.01 percentage points` | `+$1.49K` | `+$5.21K` |
| `0.1 percentage points` | `+$14.9K` | `+$52.1K` |
| `1 percentage point` | `+$149K` | `+$521K` |

Speed has its own value even if the total implementation probability stayed unchanged:

| Implementation accelerated by | Conservative personal value from avoided delay using the broad umbrella estimate ({{< var political_dysfunction_tax_per_person_annual >}}/year) |
|---|---|
| `1 year` | `+$12.6K` |
| `3 years` | `+$37.9K` |
| `5 years` | `+$63.1K` |

The same point can be stated in inverse form. If host downside is actually bounded near zero, the break-even probability lift is tiny:

| True unreimbursed human/host cost | Break-even increase in implementation probability using the full-path human benefit ({{< var wishonia_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}}) | Break-even increase using the treaty-only floor ({{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}}) |
|---|---|---|
| `$1K` | `0.0019%` | `0.0067%` |
| `$10K` | `0.019%` | `0.067%` |
| `$100K` | `0.192%` | `0.671%` |
| `$1M` | `1.92%` | `6.71%` |

Those thresholds are biased against creating the prize because they ignore two additional benefits. First, the host can receive bounded donor, fee, and implementation upside under the protocol rules above. Second, speed matters. The model's implied annual per-person opportunity cost of political dysfunction is {{< var political_dysfunction_tax_per_person_annual >}} before counting the medical timeline-shift gains, so even a one-year acceleration has large expected human value.

The delay cost can also be stated more concretely in layers.

| Layer of inaction cost | Conservative quantification | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Broad annual opportunity cost of bad allocation | {{< var political_dysfunction_tax_per_person_annual >}} per person per year | This is the cleanest single-number estimate of what humanity loses each year by leaving high-value gains unrealized. |
| Narrow direct parasitic economy visible today | ~`$1.65K` per person per year from the current {{< var global_destructive_economy_annual_2025 >}} military-plus-cybercrime drain | This is the directly observable extraction cost from the destructive economy even before counting disease drag or broader governance failure. |
| Disease drag from not curing things | ~`$1.86K` per person per year from the current 13% GDP disease burden | This is the annual cost of continuing to pay for sickness instead of curing it. |
| Direct parasitic-economy path if current growth continues | roughly `+$21.1K` per person over the next 8 years and `+$69.0K` over the next 15 years from military plus cybercrime alone | These are the cumulative direct losses on the path to the destructive economy reaching 25% of GDP in {{< var destructive_economy_years_to_25pct_gdp >}} and 50% of GDP in {{< var destructive_economy_years_to_50pct_gdp >}}. |
| Missed lifetime upside from never switching paths | {{< var treaty_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} on the conservative treaty floor; {{< var wishonia_trajectory_lifetime_income_gain_per_capita >}} on the full path | This is the conservative lower bound on what inaction costs a representative human over a remaining lifetime. |

These layers should not all be added together mechanically. The {{< var political_dysfunction_tax_per_person_annual >}} figure is the broad umbrella estimate. The parasitic-economy and disease rows are narrower visible components that make the umbrella more concrete rather than replacing it. The important point for the host decision is simpler: "do nothing" is not the zero-cost cell. It is the cell in which these losses keep compounding.

The resulting decision rule is simple: if a compatible prize instance has any non-trivial positive effect on implementation probability or implementation speed, and the host is not secretly absorbing large unreimbursed downside, hosting is the rational human choice.

### Retroactive Impact Purchasing

Bootstrap capital and project selection are different problems. Assurance contracts solve the first problem well enough: how to concentrate diffuse beneficiary capital into a treasury large enough to matter without asking organizations to spend money they do not yet have. A sponsor-underwritten dominant-assurance tranche can accelerate the first round, but it is optional. Neither version tells the treasury which downstream implementers deserve funding once the money exists.

For that layer, the prize can operate as a retroactive public-goods purchaser. Implementers fund work up front using their own capital or outside investment, produce auditable outcomes, and then sell verified impact claims back into the prize ecosystem only after the outcomes exist. In the medical domain, those claims would typically be denominated in audited DALYs averted, suffering hours avoided, or verified mortality reduction. In governance domains, they would be denominated in verified resource reallocation, durable policy adoption, or measured welfare gains under the same admissibility constraints. This preserves the paper's core logic: the prize does not pay for intentions; it pays for verified movement on the objective function.

This layer should remain downstream of the completeness rule rather than replacing it. Retroactive purchasing is a project-selection and execution market inside the already selected bundle, not a license for narrow local patches to outrank complete packages. That distinction matters. The prize first decides which complete implementation plan wins. Only then should decentralized implementers compete to supply the cheapest verified components within that plan.

## How the Payout Works

The payout should be heavily back-loaded, because your species is very good at collecting money for plans and surprisingly bad at making the plans real.

1. **Specification bounty.** A small amount for producing a complete, auditable, adversarially reviewed mechanism.
2. **Pilot bounty.** A larger amount for a live pilot that moves real money, changes real behavior, and survives contact with real institutions.
3. **Adoption bounty.** A much larger amount for statute, treaty, agency rule, ballot measure, or other binding implementation.
4. **Outcome perpetuity.** The biggest reward is a continuing share of verified recovered value, because one-time prizes create demos while ongoing revenue shares create permanent constituencies.

That is just Incentive Alignment Bonds [@iab-paper-2025] with a more brutal selection rule. Good. Brutality is appropriate here. The universe is not grading on effort.

## One Concrete Run

Abstract mechanism design is harder to trust than a visible execution trace. So here is what the Earth Optimization Plan would look like if it won.

1. The treasury raises the initial campaign pool through assurance contracts, optionally with a sponsor-underwritten dominant-assurance seed tranche, and escrows it under the no-override rules above.
2. The current bundle is submitted as a complete package: treaty wedge, dFDA / continuous evidence generation, regulatory-delay removal, IAB adoption machinery, Wishocracy preference aggregation, Optimocracy / OPG / OBG recommendation engines, and the statutory path.
3. Independent auditors score the package on admissibility. It clears because it covers every required function, beats the current DALY benchmark, and preserves the public-choice and welfare constraints.
4. The deployment layer routes capital into the first binding path with the best score-weighted return: campaign finance, legislative drafting, treaty advocacy, scorecards, and public preference collection.
5. Once one binding path succeeds, budget authority and legal authority start shifting real resources rather than merely improving discussion quality.
6. That first success funds the next missing or underpowered modules automatically through the completion covenant until the whole bundle is live.
7. Implementers then compete inside that winning bundle to supply the cheapest verified pieces, and later challengers can still replace the whole bundle if they genuinely dominate it.

That is the level of concreteness required for "implementation market" to mean more than "good intentions with a spreadsheet."

## Why Public Choice Theory Approves

Public choice theory says governments are not run by philosopher-kings. They are run by status-seeking primates inside incentive systems. Fine. Build around that.

The prize is compatible with public choice because no one has to become good:

- **Entrepreneurs** compete for a giant implementation franchise.
- **Investors** compete for a share of recovered value.
- **Politicians** compete for campaign support, better scores, reelection odds, and post-office careers.
- **Bureaucrats** compete for control of a better-funded, prestige-enhancing program instead of a shrinking one.
- **Researchers and auditors** compete for the authority to validate what works.
- **Citizens** get a simpler choice architecture and more visible returns from participation.

Nobody is asked to sacrifice self-interest. Self-interest is pointed in a better direction. More importantly, the design goal is **monotonicity**: as greed rises, capital supply, monitoring effort, political pressure, and reinvestment should all rise with it rather than collapse.

## What the Prize Selects if These Papers Are Right

If the papers in this project are broadly correct, a serious prize process will not ignore them. It will rediscover them, combine them, and then fund them because the completeness rule prevents any narrow alternative from winning unless it actually replaces the missing functions.

| Paper | What the prize uses it for | Key benchmark to beat | Why that benchmark is not insane |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|

The mechanism is statutory, not speculative: it translates measured delay into rights, deadlines, and open-data obligations. |
| **How to End War and Disease** | The integrated narrative and coalition-building wrapper around the complete Earth Optimization Plan. | Earth Optimization Plan-wide coordination at total cost of {{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}}; {{< var political_success_probability >}} estimated success probability | This is the sequencing and coalition wrapper, so its support is downstream of the already-costed modules rather than an independent giant welfare claim. |
| **Drug Development Cost Increase Analysis** [@drug-development-cost] | The proof that current regulatory structure is not merely slow but catastrophically expensive. | {{< var drug_cost_increase_pre1962_to_current_multiplier >}} cost increase since pre-1962; current average: {{< var pharma_drug_development_cost_current >}}/drug | The estimate is anchored to Baily (1972), inflation-adjusted to present dollars, and then cross-checked against six real-world comparisons, with outside estimates in the same 100-400x range. |

The large numbers in this table mostly come from three ordinary facts rather than one magical assumption: existing waste pools are already measured in trillions, regulatory delay compounds over years and across billions of people, and pragmatic evidence generation is dramatically cheaper than the legacy trial stack. The point of the table is not that every estimate is perfectly nailed down. The point is that each benchmark is at least traceable to a concrete mechanism, a concrete denominator, and a concrete empirical anchor.

In other words, the prize does not replace the Earth Optimization Plan. It sits above it and asks: *which complete package of functions wins on verified welfare per dollar?* If the answer is "this bundle," then this bundle gets implemented. If the answer is "this bundle plus one missing module," then the augmented bundle gets implemented. If the answer is "a different module set dominates row by row," then the prize funds the better design instead.

That is exactly what you want from an honest optimization process.

## The Selection Pipeline

The operational sequence is simple:

1. **Diagnose the waste.** Use the dysfunction [@political-dysfunction-tax-paper-2025] and efficiency [@us-efficiency-audit-paper-2025] papers to identify the largest pools of low-NSV spending and delay-induced harm.
2. **Generate candidate reallocations.** Use Optimocracy [@optimocracy-paper-2025], OPG [@opg-paper-2025], and OBG [@obg-paper-2025] to propose the best available moves under real-world constraints.
3. **Apply sentient-welfare guardrails.** Throw out plans that improve one metric by increasing suffering elsewhere.
4. **Aggregate preference intensity.** Use Wishocracy [@wishocracy-paper-2025] to learn what tradeoffs the public actually prefers once the options are legible.
5. **Finance adoption.** Use IAB-style structures [@iab-paper-2025] and assurance contracts to raise the capital needed to pass the highest-ranked package.
6. **Implement in the highest-ROI domain first.** At current margins that is likely medical evidence generation: pragmatic trials [@dfda-impact-paper-2025], right to trial, FDA upgrade, and continuous evidence generation [@dfda-spec-paper-2025].
7. **Reinvest recovered value.** Once a high-ROI reform starts paying, the prize treasury expands and finances the next set of reallocations.

That loop is how you get from "good idea" to "self-funding governance upgrade."

## Failover Ladder

For the Earth Optimization Plan or something better to feel inevitable, the prize cannot depend on one heroic legislative roll of the dice. It needs a failover ladder.

If the top-ranked path stalls, the treasury should automatically route capital to the next-highest admissible binding path in roughly this order:

1. treaty or national statute
2. agency rule, procurement rule, or enforcement-policy change
3. state-level legislation, interstate compact, or ballot measure
4. hospital-system, insurer, philanthropic, or employer-network adoption with auditable contractual obligations
5. narrower pilot pathways that still create legally durable precedent or reusable implementation infrastructure

The governing principle is simple: **capital may move down the ladder, but it may not sit idle**. If a higher rung becomes feasible later, the machine may move back up. If a rival package beats the incumbent at any rung while remaining complete and admissible, support migrates there instead.

That is how you turn "if this path fails, try something else" into an actual ratchet rather than a motivational slogan.

The reason the current papers likely win that first round is not sentimental attachment to the existing Earth Optimization Plan. It is that the Earth Optimization Plan combines four properties that are hard to beat simultaneously: a huge negative-NSV funding source to defund [@value-captured-by-1pct-treaty], an unusually strong risk-adjusted cost-per-DALY case [@dfda-impact-paper-2025], a concrete political-adoption mechanism [@iab-paper-2025], and a legal-regulatory path that actually opens the medical bottleneck rather than merely subsidizing the old one [@invisible-graveyard-paper-2025; @dfda-spec-paper-2025]. A challenger is free to beat that package. It just has to beat all four properties at once.

## Why This Logically Leads to These Ideas or Better

There are only three stable outcomes:

1. **The Earth Optimization Plan is best.** Then the prize selects the full baseline bundle, finances it, and implements it because $M_{complete} = 1$ is required and nothing beats it row by row.
2. **The Earth Optimization Plan is mostly right but incomplete.** Then the prize selects an augmented version of it, which still implements the existing modules while adding whatever missing function performs better.
3. **A strict improvement exists.** Then the prize selects that instead, but only if it dominates the baseline bundle function by function rather than skipping inconvenient pieces.

Those are the only serious possibilities. The unserious possibility is the one humans choose by default: endless argument with no implementation market.

Several independent lines of analysis converge on the same structural shape. Health economics says the cost-per-DALY gap between current spending and optimal spending is enormous. Public choice theory says selfish actors will move resources if you make it career-maximizing. Mechanism design says prizes with automatic replacement outperform committees. Game theory says proportional multilateral reduction is a stable equilibrium. When independent frameworks point to the same architecture, convergence is itself evidence.

The feedback loop makes this self-strengthening rather than fragile. Early success (Right to Trial passes, pragmatic trials produce cures, media covers the results, voters reward the politicians who voted for it) makes the next step cheaper. Each win creates a constituency that fights to keep it. Treaty expansion becomes easier than repeal because the bondholders, the cured patients, and the politicians who took credit all have selfish reasons to defend it.

Meanwhile, not choosing is itself a choice. The burden of treatable disease runs {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} per year. {{< var existing_drugs_efficacy_lag_deaths_total_nounit >}} people have already died from the efficacy lag alone. The status quo is not free. It is the most expensive option on the table; it merely distributes the cost across people who die quietly.

The prize is information propagation with a financing mechanism attached. Once informed self-interested actors understand the optimization is physically possible and personally profitable, their own incentives probably handle the rest. The bottleneck is not technology, not willingness, not even politics. It is the speed at which this information reaches people who can act on it.

## The Actual Objective Function

If you want the short version, it is this:

> Reward the first mechanism that can legally and durably implement every required function in the baseline bundle, or replace each one with a dominating substitute, while reallocating resources from their lowest net societal value uses to their highest ones, minimizing suffering, improving median health and wealth, and making every major affected class of living or sentient beings better off on net.

Everything else is just plumbing. And because the mechanism is agnostic to the source of suffering, as human disease cost-per-DALY rises with diminishing returns, the system naturally pivots capital to wherever suffering can be reduced most cheaply, whether that is neglected tropical diseases, factory farming, or ecosystem collapse.

That extension should be read cautiously, not mystically. The prize should only pivot beyond human disease where measurement, verification, and class-by-class welfare accounting are strong enough to clear the same admissibility tests. The point is not to authorize speculative interventions on nonhuman systems with weak evidence. The point is that once a domain can be measured rigorously enough, the prize should not remain trapped in more expensive human interventions merely because they are familiar.

And yes, this is still compatible with public choice theory, because the prize turns "find the least bad idea" into a competition for money, power, reputation, and durable institutional control. Your species already runs on those four fuels. The only innovation here is to stop burning them on things that explode.

## Conclusion

If this project is right, the prize causes its implementation. If this project is wrong, the prize discovers the better version and causes *that* implementation instead.

Either way, the feedback loop runs: more capital funds sharper selection, sharper selection funds better implementation, better implementation recovers more value, recovered value funds more capital. The mechanism does not need participants to be wise. It needs them to be greedy, impatient, and capable of reading a scoreboard.

The prize does not ask anyone to become good. It makes doing nothing the expensive option.

If there is one weird trick to ending war and disease, this is it: stop arguing about which idea is best and build a market that pays for whichever one actually works. The rest is implementation.

You are not choosing whether to optimize. You are choosing how long to wait.
